utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Before we begin the further examination of the witness, Your Honour, the Defence wishes to raise an issue concerning D65 ter 280. This is part of the KiM dossier as it's called. We have a number now, so we move that these documents be admitted into evidence. The number is D011-4582.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection, Ms. Gopalan?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D888, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd remind you the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Djordjevic continues his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have D007-0440 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll wait a little bit, and it's tab 34 in your binder. And when this document comes up, I would like you to comment on it, on the most important points in it. We now have the front page of the document. It's an indictment, a very voluminous one, so we will not go through all of it. I will simply ask you whether you are familiar with this indictment; and if so, whether you could comment on it.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indictment we now see on the screen KT number 191/94, dated the 7th of April, 1995, is familiar to me. The indictment was filed by the district public prosecutor in Pristina with the district court, and I'm familiar with the indictment because in this case in the proceedings against the persons listed in this indictment I acted as the investigating judge. Based on my investigation the public prosecutor continued criminal proceedings against these persons and filed an indictment. They are accused of the crime of conspiring to engage in hostile activities as prescribed in Article 136, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Code with the purpose of -- of violating the territorial integrity according to Article 116, paragraph 1 and engaging in terrorism under Article 125. I wish to add that I carried out an investigation against 88 persons, and after I had completed my investigation the indictment was filed against 72 persons. The Prosecutor decided not to indict 12 persons because there was insufficient evidence, so that any further criminal proceedings or investigations against these persons were stopped. From this indictment it is evident that these persons are of Albanian ethnicity, and if you look at the counts in the indictment one can establish that they're accused of engaging in the period from 1992 to 1994 in November when they were all arrested of creating a hostile association, an illegal MUP, that they had become members of this enemy association, with the aim of engaging in anti-constitutional activities to imperil the constitutional order of Yugoslavia and the territory of Serbia by planning to cede part of the -- to cut off part of the territory of the Republic of Serbia, that is, the autonomous province of Kosovo from Serbia and to accede to Albania with this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is quite enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D889, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Defence document D011-4579.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's number 37. It's not the next document in consecutive order, but I'm sure you'll find it. You can tell us what this is about now, please.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. This is a copy of the judgement handed down by the district court in Pristina. The Trial Chamber consisted of five judges, two of whom were professional judges, while the remaining three were judge jurors. The Trial Chamber handed down a judgement in connection with the indictment we saw previously against Avdija Mehmedovic and others, all of whom are listed in the preamble of this judgement. The judgement is K number 29/95 and 38/95. In this judgement the accused are found guilty. There were 72 people indicted and 69 of them were found guilty of the crime they were indicted for. I won't repeat the articles of the law, and they were sentenced to various lengths of time. And all this is described in the grounds given in the judgement. The judgement also mentions the evidence taken into consideration by the Trial Chamber and the defence put forward by the accused, and the Trial Chamber established that there had been elements of the crime of creating an illegal MUP within the scope of which there were centres of public and state security, that they had established forensic departments, operative systems, that they had conducted illegal on-site investigations in parallel with the proper institutions, that they had arrested persons of Albanian and other ethnicity, and that they had regularly sent reports to their illegal government which was acting abroad, from abroad. As I was the investigating judge in this case, a large number of exhibits were found and their numbers are listed here, the pseudonyms they used, the code books they used. The ultimate goal of their illegal activity was to have part of the territory of the FRY secede from Yugoslavia and to create a separate state in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the Trial Chamber consisting of five judges, two of whom were professional judges and three judge jurors. Could you briefly explain what this means.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the crime they were accused of and the sentence prescribed for this crime under the Law on Courts, the composition of the Trial Chamber had to consist of five members, two of whom had to be professional judges and the others were citizens of various professions who were elected as judge jurors in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D890, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what has been shown on the screen we haven't seen the date. Can we learn the date of this judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you on what page the date is to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's certainly there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will look at the overview I drew up. The date is the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 5 of the B/C/S version, if it can be shown on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's enough. We don't need to see it. We just need to hear it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The next document is D007-0541.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's tab 35, Mrs. Marinkovic. Please just comment on it briefly. It was the intention of the Defence to show how proceedings were conducted from the indictment, through the trial, to the final appeal. What do we have here?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the appeal judgement of the Supreme Court of Belgrade. It's K number I726/96 and the date is the 14th of March, 1997. In this judgement the Supreme Court of Serbia decided in the appeal against the judgement we have just seen. Some of the -- some of -- some parts of the appeal were upheld and some sentences were reduced by the Supreme Court. So some bases of appeal were upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about the composition of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chamber consisted of three professional judges. One was the Presiding Judge and the other two or members of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D891, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is D007-0562.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's number 36. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see on the screen here is a copy of the judgement with the district court in Pristina handed down in the name of the people. The number is K 37/97. The judgement was handed down on the 11th of July, 1997, and the Trial Chamber consisted of five members, two of whom were professional judges and three judge jurors. I'm familiar with this judgement because in this case I was the investigating judge against the persons indicted here. These persons were charged with the criminal offence of terrorism under Article 125 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, punishable in connection with Article 138 of the same law. In this case where I conducted the investigation, for the first time in the practice of the district court in Pristina the court -- so actually, this was the first time that the criminal offence of terrorism was investigated and tried in the district court. The investigation was conducted against 15 persons, but only three were available, only three could be arrested; and the remainder were at large. So that the investigation was carried out in their absence. An arrest warrant was issued against them, and afterwards when the indictment was filed they were tried in absentia. In this judgement where the accused are found guilty, all 15 of them, all of them are Albanians by ethnicity; and it was proved in the course of the proceedings that that they had created an enemy terrorist organisation, that they had been members of it, that the members of this organisation went for training in Albania, training in the handling of weapons. From Albania they brought weapons on to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and then they launched terrorist attacks in a certain time-period from 1993 to 1998. They launched attacks in a co-ordinated manner in various towns and villages on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Their attacks were aimed at civilians, both Albanians and non-Albanians; against members of the police; against buildings housing police stations. They attacked buildings where refugees were housed; they launched attacks from ambushes, opening fire on vehicles in which there were police officers. Their guilt was proved in the proceedings. A certain number of persons were killed, a certain number were injured. They survived but remained invalids. A certain amount of weapons were found. They attacked buildings by throwing explosive devices and hand-grenades and firing from automatic weapons. And all this was done for political motives. Their aim was to cause fear and panic among the citizens, to force Albanians who did not wish to join the KLA to do so. And a large-scale exodus of Serbs and other non-Albanians began, and their purpose was to endanger the territorial integrity of the FRY, to cut off a part of the territory, create separate state, and later on to join it up with Albania. I only wish to add one thing. One of the accused in this group who were found guilty of terrorism is Hashim Thaqi, who was tried in absentia. He was proved to be guilty of terrorism, and he was sentenced to ten years in prison. Now he is the prime minister of the so-called Independent Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you assist me, please, with the date of this conduct. The indictment seems to have been July 1997, so the conduct investigated must have been before then. Are you saying that it was found that the KLA existed and was functioning in Kosovo before July 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise. Perhaps I can provide an example as a clarification. If you look into the grounds given, you can see that there was a terrorist attack in 1993 at a railroad crossing on the road between Glogovac and Pristina. A police van was moving along that route with the policemen going to Pristina to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point of my question was not whether there was terrorist activity, but whether it was what we know as the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had existed in 1993, the terrorist gang that called itself the Kosovo Liberation Army. However, they were much smaller in numbers at the outset and then they increased their numbers, established units and staffs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Many seem to have taken the view that the Kosovo Liberation Army really came into existence as an entity in February or March 1998. I'm just very curious that you seem to identify it much earlier, even in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying that they existed as early as 1993 is because I had conducted investigations into certain cases where the accused spoke about that. When I say that it existed in 1993, I have in mind that period during which there was a group of criminals fleeing from the law. They were small in numbers and they did not pronounce openly their existence. However, the band of criminals did term themselves the KLA and started being active in the area of Drenica and Srebrenica. After that they managed to gain membership and continued with the training and activities in the field. If you take a look at the overview I showed here, I included all their terrorist actions in terms of dates, starting with 1993 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence will not have any further questions along this line of questions, although it was our original intention to put a question much similar to yours. I would like to thank you for that. I believe this was very useful. Before moving on to the next document I seek to tender this one into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D892, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The next document is D007-0356.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, Ms. Marinkovic, it is tab 38. This is another indictment. Please provide us with a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we have on the screen is an indictment issued by the district prosecutor. It was submitted against the persons stated therein. There were 21 of them in total, all Albanians. This indictment was raised after an investigation was conducted which was headed by me. The accused were charged with the crime of terrorism. As you can see in the grounds given, this group too created a terrorist association of which they were members. In the territory of Kosovo and Metohija they carried out terrorist attacks against SUP facilities as well as against facilities housing refugees and those under construction. They also attacked buildings and property owned by Albanians. In those attacks, as charged in the indictment, they premeditated -- they were accused of premeditated murder or attempts to murder several people. They caused harm to life and limb of a number of people and caused great material damage. After all the terrorist attacks described in the indictment, the terrorist organisation which called itself the KLA took on the responsibility for those attacks by issuing 29 communiques.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D893, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another indictment which is D007-0406.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it is tab 39.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we can see on the screen is another indictment raised by the district public prosecutor in Pristina after an investigation was carried out headed by myself following a request of the public district prosecutor. The accused were charged with the crime of associating in order to carry out enemy activities, and in particular crimes of terrorism as well as endangering the territorial integrity of the state. I won't go through the article numbers again since we have already mentioned that. As you can see in the left top corner, the KT number is 201/93. This concerns the group which continued its activities after a part of that group had been arrested within the illegal Ministry of National Defence. That group was -- the original group was tried in 1993, and they were pronounced guilty and received prison sentences. This group was detected later. In Pristina they published and distributed an illegal newspaper, given its contents. They advocated the creation of the state of Kosovo. Their plan was to serve the urban area and to establish guerilla units within that area. They were trained in the handling of weapons so as to be ready once the KLA initiated their attacks. They would then use those guerilla units to carry out attacks against citizens in towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D894, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We will move on to the next topic, which I am inclined to title Racak. This will bring us closer to the close of this examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D149.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it is tab 40. This is an Official Note. Let's go through it to see what it is, who drafted it, when, why; in brief, the details.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Official Note we have on the screen is mine. I put it together as an investigating judge. It is number 14/99. It states that on the 15th of January, 1999, I tried to enter the village of Racak so as to carry out an on-site investigation concerning a previous terrorist attack which occurred there. I was prevented from completing the investigation because after we had entered the village of Racak fire was opened at us from different types of weapons forcing us to turn back. In this note it is stated that on that day I was informed by the duty service of the Urosevac MUP that there had been a terrorist attack in Racak and that I was supposed to decide whether there should be an on-site investigation or not. Before setting out from Pristina for Stimlje in the police station from which we were supposed to go further afield and eventually reaching Racak, I was visited by the deputy district prosecutor in my office, Mr. Ismet Sufta. He was on duty that day like I was. He agreed with me that we were to go there to conduct that investigation. Once we reached the Stimlje police station, we were awaited there by Mr. Janicijevic, who was the chief of the secretariat. He shared with us the information as to what had happened that morning. He told us that in the early hours of the 15th of January, 1999, there was a clash between the police and members of a terrorist gang in the village of Racak, which was their stronghold including Racak and its surrounding villages. Given that the policemen had already secured the scene to create the preconditions for our on-site investigation, the chief used radio communication to get in touch with them. At a certain point in time, he was informed that there is a lull, that there was no sporadic firing from the hills, and that the team could indeed go to Racak to conduct that on-site investigation. Together with the other members of the team and escorted by the police, I went to the village of Racak. As I state here, we arrived there at around 2.00 p.m. By the policemen on the spot I was informed that they collected all of the weapons they could find in the nearby hills. All the weapons were put in a single spot. Together with the prosecutor and other team members such as scene of crime officers and the general crime inspector who was there, we saw all the weapons there. I specified the items found in terms of weapons, military uniforms, ammo crates with the ammunition of different calibres. We also found a Browning machine-gun, the calibre of which is 12.7 millimetre and another Browning machine-gun, the calibre of which was 7.9, 36 automatic rifles, two sniper rifles, five hand-held rocket-launchers, 12 mines --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 12 mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 22 hand-grenades, radio stations, hand-held radios, medical equipment, as well as military equipment bearing KLA insignia. All the weapons were found there and photographed. I ordered the police to load the weapons into the vehicle. After everything was done, we inspected the area, searching for any casualties. However, at that point in time they opened fire on us. The police advised me that it would be a risky thing to proceed for reasons of safety, and they recommended that we turn back. We indeed did so. While returning from Racak one could hear sporadic firing from the nearby villages; however, we managed to reach the Stimlje police station safe and sound. We agreed that the next day, on the 16th, we were to go to Stimlje again and to attempt another on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was on the 15th. I will have a number of other questions, one of which will be slightly off on a tangent, but I believe it is rather important. You mentioned the public prosecutor who visited the scene with you that day. I believe his name was Ismet Sufta. Who were the prosecutors during the NATO air campaign with the district prosecutor's office in Pristina, and did they observe the same schedule as the municipal and district courts, or were they organised in a different fashion?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the district prosecutor's office there was a single district prosecutor who was the head of the office. He had his deputies, five or six of them. They followed his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the district prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Stefanovic was the district prosecutor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who the deputies were, at least the names of those whom you can remember and whom you worked with?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Jovanovic was one, then Miodrag Surla, Dragomir Zivic [as interpreted], Ismet Sufta, Ljiljana Delic, and Radojka Vlahovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they all continue working throughout the war, all six of them plus the head of the office?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The district prosecutor remained in his position as well as Ismet Sufta. For a while Dragan Zivic worked as well. Before that Jovica Jovanovic and Miodrag Surla went to join the military prosecutor's office. They were later joined by Dragan Zivic. Ljiljana and Radojka, the female colleagues, since they had minor children, were not under work obligation and they left Pristina for security reasons with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will go back to your Official Note. Upon entering the village of Racak when you observed the village houses, could you notice any damage caused by any heavy weapons on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that first day, I did not notice any type of damage on the houses which could indicate that there had been shelling or heavy pieces engaged there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is as follows: When you went to carry out this on-site investigation, did you notice any fortifications, trenches, dugouts, or anything of that sort? Did you have time to observe anything like that on that day?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day we did not manage to tour the terrain so that apart from the weapons we seized on the site we were not able to observe anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: During the investigation were there any local people in the village?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see that the village was deserted, that there was no one around. We saw no people or animals. I gained the impression that the population had been moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As this is the 15th of January, 1999, just before the NATO air-strikes against the FRY, you said that the police had to inform the international observers in line with the agreement reached. Do you know whether they did so?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Pristina when I was informed by the SUP duty service that an incident had occurred in the village of Racak and that we had to carry out an investigation, I reminded the duty service that they should immediately inform the headquarters of the OSCE and that they should go to Stimlje, where we would meet up and go to Racak together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But were there any members from the OSCE waiting for you in Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You decided that on the next day you would again go on that site, that was the 16th of January. What did you do on that day? Did the same prosecutor go with you? Did the same police officers secure the spot? What happened on the 16th of January, to the best of your recollection and based on this note?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, as agreed with the members of my team, we set out from Pristina to Stimlje. This was at around 10.00 or 10.30 a.m., and we arrived in Stimlje and first went to the police station there in order to find out whether it was safe to proceed to Racak and whether the police could guarantee our safety while conducting the investigation. When we arrived in Racak, or rather -- no, when we arrived in the Stimlje police station, everything was quiet. As Racak is nearby and we could not hear any shots being fired from afar, I set out with my team escorted by the police to the village of Racak. On the road, however, as soon as we turned off the main road going from Stimlje to Prizren and Urosevac, hardly had we arrived halfway, fire was opened on us from all directions so that we turned back. And on that day we did not manage to get to the village or carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall anything special about that day, the 16th of January, and Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, as we did not manage to carry out an on-site investigation, we went back to Stimlje police station and again in agreement with the prosecutor and the other members of the team we decided that on the following day, the 17th of January, we would try again. We then set out towards Pristina from Stimlje and we all went home. In the evening when I switched on my television the first news item I saw showed Mr. Walker -- a picture of him entering the village of Racak with members of the OSCE --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. You saw this on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 16th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please go on. I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard Walker saying that there had been a massacre in Racak. I was speechless, dumbfounded. Walker had entered Racak before the official and authorised on-site investigation team, which had been prevented from carrying out its work. Walker had entered Racak on his own, without any agreement or consultation with us and made the statement that a massacre had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened on the 17th of January?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of January, together with the members of the investigation team - and I also invited a forensic expert, Dr. Slavisa Dobricanin, who was the director of the forensic institute in Pristina, and he joined the team, I thought I might need his help in case I was able to carry out an on-site investigation on that day and in case we found any corpses. At the police station in Stimlje, where we arrived in the afternoon, and both on the 16th and the 17th, the duty service had informed the representatives of the OSCE that they should come to Stimlje police station at a certain time if they wanted to join me and the other members of the investigation team and go with us to the village of Racak to carry out the inspection. On the 16th no one from the OSCE was there, but on the 17th when we arrived at the police station in Stimlje, upstairs in the office of the chief members of the OSCE led by Walker's deputy, a British General John Drewienkiewicz arrived there. After introductions I told them that if the security conditions were in place we would go to the village of Racak and carry out an on-site investigation. When the English general, John, heard that he raised his voice and started issuing orders to me. I was surprised by this. I couldn't believe it. I can say here that the only person who ever tried to influence my work or prevent me from carrying out my job as an investigating judge was General Drewienkiewicz, who had no right to do that. He told me angrily that I could not go to Racak, that I could go to Racak only with him and without a police escort, that in Racak there were local people who would be frightened if they saw the police, that they would open fire on the police, and I said to him, "If you say that there are local people there, why would they open fire? Are the local villagers armed or not? If they are armed, are they villagers or are they soldiers?" He was even more irritated by what I said and he said, "You must not go to Racak because if you do there will be more victims. The 'villagers' will open fire. I will inform my chief Walker and tell him to stop you from doing this." I tried to explain to him that no one could prevent me from going to Racak and carrying out an on-site investigation because that was my duty as an investigating judge. I already knew that there had been an incident in Racak, I had been informed of that officially, and it was my duty to carry out an on-site investigation and establish what had happened on the spot, search for evidence, establish whether there were any casualties, how many, and what they had died of. He became even angrier when he saw how persistent I was, and he threatened me. He said if I entered the village and if innocent villagers got killed, he would report me to the ICTY, and I would be responsible if any more people got killed. There we parted ways. He decided not to go. He withdrew with the other members of his team, and I set out with the members of my team and a police escort to the village of Racak. When we set out to the village of Racak we came as far as the entrance to the village. Fire was opened on us again from all directions. Shooting started so we could not turn back, but we did and we were fired at all the way. On that day there was damage to an institution for retarded children, the health care clinic, the police station, and an official vehicle which was parked in the yard of the police station. We did not manage to carry out an on-site investigation on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll pause here. The next exhibit, or rather, document is dated the 18th of January, and I move that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I see that it is already a Defence exhibit. My mistake. Thank you. We will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the Defence exhibit number? Is that D149?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again. The next document is D48.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 148. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. It's in your binder number 41.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see here on the screen is a record of the on-site investigation. The number is KRI 14/99. I drew up this report concerning the on-site investigation I carried out on the 18th of January, 1999, in the village of Racak when we managed to enter the village of Racak on the fourth day. The members of the on-site investigation team are listed, and we see here that the investigation commenced at 1400 hours. As on the previous days, I and the members of the investigation team set out from Pristina to Stimlje in a car. When we arrived at Stimlje we first went to the police station there. This was at around noon or 12.30. We were met by the chief of the secretariat and we spoke to him, asking him what the situation was on the ground and whether the conditions would be in place for us to go on site. The chief of the branch [as interpreted] police station, Mitic, was in the office with the chief of the secretariat. He was there and he was following what was going on. The chief had a radio station, by means of which he communicated with the policemen who were at Racak. While we were talking there, after about half an hour or 20 minutes, General Djordjevic entered the office. We were introduced to him. That was the first time I had met him, and he spoke to the chief of the secretariat to learn whether the conditions were in place and whether the team could go on site and carry out an on-site investigation. The chief of the secretariat, Janicijevic, described the situation to him but I wasn't paying much attention to all the details. After a while, the chief of the secretariat told us that he had been informed from the ground that there was a lull, that it was currently quiet in the village, that we could set out in order to try to carry out an on-site investigation on that day. With my colleague, the prosecutor, and Sasa Dobricanin, the court forensic expert, I left the building of the police station, when I was approached by representatives of the OSCE. They told me they had arrived and that they wanted to go with us if the conditions were in place for carrying out an investigation on that day. These were two Americans and one Italian, and they had an interpreter interpreting from English into Serbian and vice versa. I entered their names into the record. When we were about to set out, everyone entered their own vehicle, and Mitic, the chief of the branch police station, came down and said he would go with us. He said that he had been told to do so by Janicijevic, his chief of secretariat. In view of the fact the situation had been risky and unsafe on the previous days, he was supposed to escort us and provide for our security in case there was any firing or any risk. We set out in a convoy and arrived at Racak. There was no shooting along the way. When we entered the village of Racak, left our vehicles, and started towards the village, one of the police officers who was already there approached me and told me that there were bodies in the mosque. Together with the investigation team, the representatives of the OSCE, so all of us together, we entered the mosque and we all viewed the bodies in the mosque together. In the mosque, as I stated in this report, we saw 40 bodies; 39 of whom were men, and one was a woman. The bodies were lined up. They were all dressed. They had shoes which looked like military boots. Some had dark grey, others navy blue military trousers, and they had military belts on those trousers. The forensic technician, acting on my orders, numbered the bodies. They were photographed. Dr. Dobricanin inspected each body visually and immediately stated out loud that there were no traces of any slaughter on those bodies. On one or two bodies there was damage to the head -- injuries to the head, where the forensic experts said these had been caused by birds or animals because the corpses had lain outdoors for a while. After the corpses had been photographed, each body was put into a separate body-bag according to the proper procedure, and they were placed in a refrigerator truck which was immediately sealed in the presence of the OSCE. And this refrigerator truck containing 40 bodies on my orders went immediately to the Forensic Institute in Pristina, there to await further instructions from me as the investigating judge. After this, as it was quiet, there was no shooting, we were not hindered by anyone, we went on to inspect the terrain and see what other evidence we could find. We thought we might find other corpses or perhaps the pit I had seen on television where Walker had shown bodies lying there, saying that allegedly there had been a massacre. When we set out on foot along the hill we immediately came across trenches, and following those trenches we arrived at an abandoned house. When we entered that house we found various objects, which gave us to understand that the KLA headquarters had been located there. We found weapons, uniforms, lists, duty rosters of members of the KLA. In the yard next to the house where the headquarters had been, we found a store of food, large quantities of flour, cigarettes, eggs. We found a kitchen where food was prepared and where there were tables and chairs. It gave us the impression that large numbers of people had eaten there. In the house itself we found mortars for hand-held rocket-launchers, seven rounds of ammunition, a large quantity of bullets, three hand-grenades, trousers, and green vest with hand-grenades and bullets in the pockets as well as propaganda material. Everything that was found in that house was photographed, numbered, labelled, recorded, and I entered all this into my record. And then these items were seized for further investigation and forensic work. When we continued on our way, we followed the trenches which ran from the bottom of the hill to the top on both the right-hand side and left-hand side. In the trenches we found very many spent shell casings or cartridges. We found the tools that had been used to dig these trenches, and we found parts of uniforms here and there. When we reached the top of the hill, which was known as Vis, we found a machine-gun nest. A big room had been dug into the hill which contained a stove which could be used to burn wood. We found wooden beds, military blankets, coats, jackets, and trousers, and all around there was a large quantity of spent cartridges made in China. There was a military canvas there as well as a tripod for the machine-gun. It was all included in our note about the on-site investigation, and all the items were taken away to be used as evidence. Throughout the investigation the OSCE observers accompanied us. They did not try to interfere with our work. They only occasionally put questions, and I provided answers with the assistance of their interpreter. Throughout the investigation one of the scene of crime officers was tasked with video recording everything we found. We toured most of that village and the entire village. We did not, however, manage to locate the pit that Walker indicated in the broadcast. We tried to follow another route going downhill on the other side, trying to find the pit; however, having reached the foot of the hill, we were still unable to find any other casualties or traces of massacre or blood. When we went back to the village centre, we were still walking between the houses when fire was opened at us. I'm not a soldier, but there was firing all around from different types of weapons, I believe. There were bullets zooming about. We were trying to take cover. It was so risky and basically none of us believed we would get out of there alive. We ran downhill any which way we could, and we tried to take shelter in the house together with the OSCE representatives. We, however, did not manage to reach the house because the firing was so strong we had to lie down. We managed to reach our vehicles. We got in and left the village as quickly as possible. The fire continued throughout. At a certain point along our route, we felt that something had struck our vehicle, the vehicle where the forensic expert and I were. The vehicle was lifted off the ground and fell down again. The vehicle was indeed hit, but fortunately enough no one was injured. We managed to reach the police station eventually and tried to calm down. We took our time to recover before eventually leaving Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion did you encounter any villagers in Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I just wanted to point something out. Page 21, line 25, it is stated there that Mitic was the chief of the branch police station, but he was actually the chief of the police station, not a branch police station. This was clearly a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Mitic was the chief of the police department in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance. There seemed to be something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have D002-0952.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it is tab 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that on the screen. My associate is informing me that the number is incorrect. D003-0952. I apologise. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is on the screen now. Could you please provide a comment. It is your tab 42.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a list of those identified who had been killed in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have anything to tell us regarding this list, something in particular which may be something you observed? First of all, who identified the bodies, and were there any other examinations conducted on those corpses?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the 40 corpses we found, since we did not know their identity, I issued an order to the forensic service to identify the bodies by taking finger-prints which were to be used alongside their identity documents and other files to ascertain their identity clearly. Before that, I issued another instruction which was followed upon the very next. It was when we unsealed the refrigerator truck in the presence of OSCE representatives. The bodies were then taken to the forensic medical institute and paraffin glove samples were taken from all the corpses from the mosque in order to establish whether there were any gunpowder traces on their hands. After that, an order was issued to the forensic medical institute to carry out the autopsies of those bodies. The scene of crime service which took the finger-prints managed to identify all of the bodies. We have their first and last names contained in this document as well as their dates of birth. This concerns the 40 bodies we identified which had been found in the mosque in Racak. Concerning this list I can tell you that when I testified as a Defence witness in the case against Mr. Milosevic I was shown a list from the indictment. On that list there were 42 names. It was the first time that I learned that another figure is being used, the figure being 45, although I am certain that there were only 40 corpses that we found in the mosque. Later on, with the assistance of the Trial Chamber and the prosecutor, we established what the differences were between the lists. In the list of 45 there were people who were not found in the mosque at all. We, therefore, corrected the list, bringing it closer to the original list of 40 which I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the results of the paraffin glove test concerning the mortal remains that were tested?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received a report concerning that. It was established that 37 corpses contained gunpowder traces. Only three had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You told me you issued an order to carry out autopsies. Who did that on the mortal remains in question?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The autopsy of those mortal remains found in the village of Racak was carried out by a Yugoslav team of eminent experts, pathologists, and forensic medical experts. Two Belarus pathologists also participated as part of the team. They were in Pristina at the time because they were carrying out autopsies of other corpses. Later on a Finnish pathology team joined in. They were not present at the outset. After their arrival from Finland they joined in, following my agreement and those experts who were already working on the corpses agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who headed the Finnish team?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Helena Ranta.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question before the break. Did you establish the identity of the female found in the mosque in Racak; and if so, could you please tell us who she was? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identity of the female corpse was established. Her name was Hanusha Mehmeti [phoen]. My operational information I received from the prosecutor's office indicates that she was the sister of two KLA members. Her father was also a KLA member in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly wish to have this document admitted. After the break I will have only a little bit of time left, which I will use well to conclude my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document you want admitted is the list? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D895, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next document, I wanted to go back to a topic we discussed before briefly only. Ms. Marinkovic, when you entered Racak on the 15th of January the first time and when you came back on the 18th -- well, first I asked you about the 15th whether you were able to observe any damage on the houses, and the same question now goes for the 18th. Did you observe any damage caused by heavy weapons on the buildings in Racak, and did you notice any other types of destruction such as houses which were burned or things similar to that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any traces of shelling or of any houses being set ablaze. I didn't notice that on the 15th, on the 16th, the 17th, and the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have D003-0959.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it is tab 43. I believe you have already commented on a similar thing during your testimony. I would kindly ask you for your comment now as well.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document has to do with the forensic examination of the scene of incident which forms part of the on-site investigation report. This was done following the instructions of the competent judge. It was carried out by a forensic technician of the Urosevac SUP who was present there. He was a member of the on-site investigation team. In this report it is stated what activities were taken by the expert and what instructions they received from the judge. We also have certain photographs showing weapons, although the pictures are not of a very good quality. However, it contains the weapons found at the 15th of January, 1999. That is to say the first day when we entered the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is sufficient. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this Defence document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not been able to follow this document, since we've only had the cover page. So I'm not clear on what the witness has been commenting on. Are there separate pages behind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would assume so, but can you tell us, Mr. Djordjevic, how many pages are in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. In the B/C/S there are nine pages, in the English document it is only six pages, probably due to a smaller font.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there also photographs and other attachments?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the photographs and records from the crime scene by the scene of crime officers. If Ms. Gopalan is still not satisfied, we can go through each and every page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We think it would be useful to quickly view each page of the document. We'll arrange that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar is also confirming that that would be possible. The first page seems to be the same in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next page. The next page in the English. Can you keep going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D896, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The next document in your binder is tab 44. It is Defence document D003-0989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is a record of damage on the court vehicle, the damage was sustained on the way back.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the cover page of the case file of the Urosevac SUP. Inside the file there are photographs of the vehicle, that the vehicle was damaged on the 18th of January, 1999, when the on-site investigation team was returning from the scene, the vehicle was fired upon. And we see a detailed description of the damage. This is also a report of an examination of the vehicle which forms part of the case file. There's also a report from the scene as well as all the other measures we undertook in Racak between the 15th and the 18th of January, 1999. This particular page has to do with the 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I presume there are also photographs in the file?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the Court and the Prosecution each page of the B/C/S and English versions of the document plus the photographs. In other words, let's go through this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence moves to have this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D897, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is D003-0951.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's tab 45, Madam. Could you please comment on this document which we see before us? Could you explain to the Court what sort of document this is, on what occasion it was compiled, who compiled it, and all the other details concerning this document?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we see on the screen is an order issued by the investigating judge to the forensic technicians of the Pristina court, ordering them to do the following: In co-operation with the group of forensic experts who are conducting autopsies on bodies in the institute of forensic medicine in Pristina do a paraffin glove test of each body individually, do gunpowder tests on the body and clothing, perform dactyloscopy to establish the identity of the bodies, to photograph each body separately, conduct the forensic examination of each projectile and other foreign body found in the bodies in order to establish the type of projectile and weapon involved. And under item 2 it says that the above investigative action shall be carried out by authorised forensic technicians of the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you tender that, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but in e-court there are some other documents bearing the same number. So can we go through this page by page, as we did in the previous case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the rest is not in e-court, so I do tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps the judge could help us. We see nothing in this order about autopsies. Now, is there a separate order for those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it this order was given on the 19th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That appears in the B/C/S form but not in the English translation. It appears there is just this page, Mr. Djordjevic. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D898, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that this is the only page in e-court. I will have to put the following question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a special order to conduct autopsies of the bodies found in the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To whom was the order to conduct autopsies issued?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was issued to the commission of forensic experts and pathologists at the level of Yugoslavia. Slavisa Dobricanin was the head of that group, and the members included Dr. Otasevic from Nis; Dr. Dunjic from Belgrade; Dr. Tasic from Novi Sad; and Dobricanin from Pristina. These were all forensic experts, pathologists, and also a two-member team from Belarus whose names I cannot recall, but they are listed in the order. And the order also states what is to be established in the autopsy of all 40 bodies. At the end of that order it says that a Finnish team of forensic experts would join in the autopsy once they arrive from Finland.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the investigation did you receive any conclusions from the forensic team?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After an autopsy was conducted on all 40 bodies, I received a joint conclusion from the forensic experts, which was the same in the case of all three teams, the Yugoslav team, the Belarus team, and the Finnish team. The conclusion was that the cause of death of all the bodies were injuries they sustained from fire-arms, hand-held weapons, and that they had been shot from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll pause now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the meantime could we have document D003-0955 on the screen. Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was some confusion here. This document is in your binder under the same tab you have just been looking at, 40. This is the general conclusion you have just mentioned. Did these general conclusions ensue after the order you had issued?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these conclusions it says that it was established that the cause of death in all 40 bodies were projectiles, that all the injuries had been fatal except in the case of six bodies, where there had also been injuries caused by animals after death, post mortem. The wounds were found in various parts and sides of the bodies, had arrived from different directions. And that all the body wounds were accompanied by corresponding rips on the clothing of the dead bodies. Then there is a description of how the team worked, that the autopsies were videotaped with two or three video cameras in the presence of the European community and the Finnish team, that they had been photographed, sketched, and the injuries described in the course of the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 2 of this document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May we go on?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these joint conclusions, in item 12 it says that the Finnish team of experts which joined in later on examined all 16 bodies on which autopsies had been performed before their arrival, and after that they continued working together with the other teams on the autopsies that were conducted afterwards. The date here is the 30th of January, 1999, and the conclusions were signed by the Yugoslav team of experts and the experts from Belarus. And we can see their names and signatures here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence wishes to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D899, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have D003-0949. I think we have the complete documentation now as regards this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see on the monitor now is the order I issued to conduct an autopsy of the dead bodies, listing what had to be established and who was to participate in the autopsy. And it states here that the cause of death should be established, the type and nature of the injuries and when they were inflicted for each body individually, defects in the clothing, and whether they were consistent with the injuries on the body for each body individually; on the basis of gunpowder analysis, whether the damage to the clothing contained traces of gunpowder particles or whether the damage to the clothing was caused later. Every projectile and other foreign body was to be photographed and sent to the competent organs to establish what kind of projectile it is. After the autopsy, establish if there are identical items of clothing or footwear and determine the manufacturer. This order also contains an instruction that technicians of the Pristina SUP should be allowed to conduct a paraffin glove test, a gunpowder analysis both of the body and of the clothing, and to carry out dactyloscopy in order to establish identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think this will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D900, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, on receipt of this forensic report, was it necessary to carry out any further investigation? Can you tell us what happened after this?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I received the written report on the results of the forensic investigations I had ordered, I sent the complete file to the prosecutor of the district court in Pristina for further action. That was my duty under the Law on Criminal Procedure. The complete file was sent to the prosecutor of the district court in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And that was the end of your investigation in this case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I undertook all investigative activities that I as an investigating judge was able to undertake in connection with the events in Racak. Before that, no investigation had been instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have D61 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please comment on this document briefly.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it was sent to the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia by the Pristina secretariat on the 10th of December, 1998. As for the contents, I can see that this has to do with an investigation carried out by me as the investigating judge as well as other members of the scene of crime -- on-site investigation. I was supposed to undertake that investigation on the 10th of December, 1998, in the village of Obrinje. Concerning this event, I can tell you that the district court in Pristina received a request from a number of families which lived in Gornje Obrinje. They reported that in Gornje Obrinje some of their family members who had been killed were buried. Following that request, I set a date for the investigation. Concerning the exhumation of the corpses, we also included forensic medical institute experts. We needed their assistance for the exhumations, and Ms. Helena Ranta also headed a Finnish team which came along. We agreed with the Finnish team to go there on the 10th of December early in the morning, escorted by the police. They were in charge of securing the perimeter. We set out from Pristina to Obrinje. On approaching the village of Obrinje, the vehicle where the Finnish pathologists were stopped. They all got out of the vehicle, together with Ms. Helena Ranta. Not knowing what it was about, I got out of my vehicle and with the assistance of an interpreter I inquired about why they had stopped. Helena Ranta told us that we cannot go any further towards Gornje Obrinje in that composition. She said that there was a barricade at Gornje Obrinje manned by armed KLA members. If they saw the police they would open fire, endangering us. She suggested that I alone accompany them in their vehicle. When I asked who was there to guarantee my safety, she said that she couldn't do that because if they opened fire she could be hit. I put the second question then, telling her that I could not carry out an on-site investigation without my team members and that on-site investigations have to be undertaken by the competent authorities of Serbia. There should also be a forensic expert and the police was supposed to be there to secure the scene. She did not want to go on in the presence of the police, and we were unable to reach an agreement on how to proceed and whether there would be an exhumation that day. It was already getting dark, and we noticed that in the surrounding hills since we were down on the road terrorists began appearing and surrendering -- and surrounding us. They wore black uniforms and had weapons. It was only a matter of time when they would open fire. Since we were unable to agree that I alone should accompany them or that they themselves can carry out the on-site investigation without any authority, we agree that we should go back that day to Pristina. We also agreed that we should return to Gornje Obrinje and were supposed to agree on a date. However, after that Helena Ranta did not come back, she never asked for another date. And the families were no longer requesting any investigations. I drafted an Official Note about all that, but it remained in the district court in Pristina. I do not have a copy which I can produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's Exhibit D61 already?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sorry. That's my fault. [Interpretation] The next Defence document is D011-4530.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 47, Ms. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Due to the lack of time, we were unable to secure a translation; however, he we will receive one. This is the first page of the document. Could we please go to page 3. I believe that is a criminal report. Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please comment since there was something specific in relation to this document, and can you also refer to the time-period, please.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have on the screen is a copy of the criminal report sent by the Pristina SUP to the district public prosecutor. It was submitted against an unidentified perpetrator charged with the crime of murder contained in Article 47 of the penal code of Serbia. The victim was Bajram Kelmendi and his two sons Kastriot and Kustrima from Pristina. The crime was committed on the 26th of March, 1999, in Pristina, during the period of NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What else can you tell us about the victims?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Bajram Kelmendi personally. He was a good attorney in Pristina dealing with criminal cases only. I had a good co-operation, a professional co-operation, with him. Unfortunately, this is what happened to him. Concerning this event on the 26th of March, 1999, as the investigating judge following information I received from the duty service about the whereabouts of the corpses, I attended the crime scene. I drafted a report, the number of which is 84/99. In the report I specify the place where the corpses were found, in the proximity of the Energoinvest company. I described the position of the bodies, the clothes, as well as the 35 spent cartridges on the scene from a 7.62-millimetre weapon. This was all taken as evidence. At the on-site investigation scene, he Ejup Golica was also present. He was the victim's brother-in-law. He recognised both Bajram and his two sons. He was able to identify them, following which I ordered the forensic medical institute to conduct autopsies of these three bodies. They were subsequently transferred to the institute. Photographs were taken of the crime scene and sketches made because there was also a scene of crime officer in attendance. I sent a copy of the on-site investigation report to the district public prosecutor for further action. In this case, as the investigating judge, I was in charge of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the perpetrators were ever discovered?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question put by Defence today has to do with the processing of crimes committed by specifically MUP members. I won't ask you about any army members because you have already explained that this was within the competence of the military court. As of the moment of your appointment as investigating judge in 1994, do you know of any MUP members being processed or prosecuted by the Pristina court? You, as you said, were an investigating judge with that court as of 1994.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that during that period there were criminal procedures and proceedings instituted against MUP members. Investigations were carried into those cases by myself or my colleagues, although I don't know how many specifically and who the persons involved were since it's been a long time since. However, I know that after the completion of investigations, indictments were issued against those who perpetrators those crimes and that judgements were handed down as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence seeks to tender this last document. At the same time we wish to thank the witness for coming here in order to clarify some issues important for Defence. With this I close my examination-in-chief, Your Honours. Of course this should be MFI'd, given that a translation is still pending, as I have already informed you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The criminal report will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D901, MFI'd, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago we had some testimony in relation to the incident in Gornje Obrinje. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already shared with you the things I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's right. Am I right that in this case, the Gornje Obrinje incident, an on-site investigation was never completed?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not completed because we were prevented from attending the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that the families were no longer requesting any investigations, correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: As an investigating judge, did you have an obligation to complete an investigation even if the family members did not require or request an investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigative measure of on-site investigation in Gornje Obrinje is something I attempted to carry out; however, I was prevented in doing so. Given that Helena Ranta herself told me that there were KLA members there, for objective reasons this could not be completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just a few more questions on your role, on your obligations, as an investigating judge. You testified about these obligations in the Milosevic trial. You've already mentioned in this case that you were -- you provided testimony in the Milosevic case. As I understand it, an investigating judge, you said, makes no conclusions and as an investigating judge you collect evidence. Is that correct? We can call up the Milosevic testimony if that's necessary to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need. What I said is true. As an investigating judge I am not there to make conclusions. I merely collect evidence following a request of the competent district prosecutor or if I deem it to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So your duty was to observe, record, and collect evidence in a crime scene, and it was the prosecutor who made the decision whether to take the case forward. And I'm reading from your testimony in Milosevic now. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to some cases we spoke about earlier today, for example, D892. That's the exhibit number for a case judgement rendered on 11 July 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could call up that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you recall this case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this case you mentioned today line 8, 7, saying that: "The aim of these defendants was to cause fear and panic among the citizens, to force Albanians who did not wish to join the KLA to do so." And you go on to say that: "The purpose was to endanger the territorial integrity of the FRY and to cut off a part of the territory, create a separate state, and later on to join up with Albania." Now, how did you know this was the aim of the defendants?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the defendants themselves when interviewed during the investigation openly spoke about that. They proudly discussed their idea of creating an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, a similar goal was stated by the defendants in the illegal MUP case. Do you remember that case, D890? Do you remember the illegal MUP case? If not I can call up the document.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the document. Put your question, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And the question is --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it doesn't need to be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- these defendants as well, you said, had the goal of creating a separate state. In this case as well, was this information that was provided to you during the interviews?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
